research.job_description_summary: Wipro's official early-careers page lists the Elite programme (newly graduated engineers) and the Turbo programme (engineering talent from 46 named institutes, including IIITs and NITs), among others, but gives no selection stages or skills. Secondary sources describe the National Level Talent Hunt (NLTH) online test (aptitude, essay, and per one source a coding section), followed by a technical and an HR interview. Elite is described as the Project Engineer track (about 3.5 LPA) and Turbo as a higher track.
required_skills: Programming fundamentals (C, C++, Java or Python)
limitations: The official Wipro early-careers page names the programmes but describes no selection stages, exam pattern or required skills; a sample official Project Engineer posting (2025) is for a mechanical design role and is not relevant to fresher software hiring.

Sources disagree on the NLTH pattern: one guide says aptitude plus an essay and two coding questions, another says aptitude (about 20 questions, 60 minutes) plus an essay with coding only in the technical interview. Coding rounds are therefore labeled REPORTED.

The Unstop article (updated 2026-03-06) and the JobRise guide (2026-02-11) are editorial lists; their questions are not attributed to individual candidates, so most items here are original practice questions (class D) using those lists as topic context.
Only two items come from explicitly attributed candidate anecdotes inside the JobRise guide (a HashMap question and a Java memory-model question); each is a single report.
The 15-month service agreement, package figures, cutoffs and the Turbo role title (Senior Project Engineer) come from secondary sources and were not confirmed on Wipro's own pages.
Turbo hiring is restricted to named institutes, so Turbo content may not apply to all candidates.

Evidence handling: practice questions cite no sources; where a source only supplied topic context it is named in the question notes. Practice and job-description-inferred questions are UNVERIFIED and capped at LOW confidence on import.

Review status: answers, samples and cited counts come from the researcher and were not independently re-run; spot checks only. Source titles and some dates are blank because the sources did not show them.

questions.prompt: How does a HashMap work internally? What happens on a collision?
questions.relevance_to_role: A Manipal candidate account in a 2026 guide says a HashMap question caused the candidate to freeze.
questions.expected_answer: Keys are hashed to bucket indexes; each bucket holds a list (or tree after many collisions in modern Java). On collision, entries are chained and equals() picks the right key. Resizing rehashes when the load factor is exceeded. Average get/put is O(1).
follow_ups: Why must you override hashCode when you override equals?
questions.notes: Single anecdotal candidate account inside an editorial guide.

questions.prompt: Explain how memory is allocated in Java: stack, heap and where objects and variables live.
questions.relevance_to_role: An SRM candidate account in a 2026 guide mentions a Java memory-model question.
questions.expected_answer: Local variables and method calls live on the stack (one per thread); objects live on the heap, which the garbage collector manages. References on the stack point to heap objects; static data lives in the method area/metaspace.
follow_ups: What causes OutOfMemoryError?
common_mistakes: Saying objects live on the stack
questions.notes: Single anecdotal candidate account inside an editorial guide.

questions.prompt: Explain polymorphism using classes Animal, Dog and Cat. Show run-time polymorphism.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between encapsulation and abstraction?
questions.relevance_to_role: Encapsulation versus abstraction is listed by an editorial source.
questions.expected_answer: Encapsulation bundles data with methods and restricts access (private fields, getters). Abstraction exposes only essential behaviour and hides complexity (interfaces, abstract classes). Encapsulation is about protection; abstraction about simplification.
follow_ups: Give a real-life example of each.
questions.notes: Topic comes from an editorial list that does not attribute the question to a candidate; the item itself is an original practice question. Topic context only (no candidate attribution): https://unstop.com/blog/wipro-elite-national-talent-hunt-interview-questions/amp.

questions.prompt: What is normalization? Explain 1NF, 2NF and 3NF with a short example.
questions.relevance_to_role: Normalization is listed by editorial sources for the Wipro technical interview.
questions.expected_answer: Normalization reduces redundancy and anomalies. 1NF: atomic values. 2NF: 1NF and no partial dependence on part of a composite key. 3NF: 2NF and no transitive dependence of non-key attributes. Example: split an Orders table into Customers and Orders.
follow_ups: When would you denormalize?
questions.notes: Topic comes from an editorial list that does not attribute the question to a candidate; the item itself is an original practice question. questions.prompt: What is the difference between DDL and DML commands? Give examples.
questions.relevance_to_role: DDL versus DML is listed by an editorial source.
questions.expected_answer: DDL defines structure (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE); DML manipulates data (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT is often grouped with DQL). DDL is generally auto-committed; DML can be rolled back in a transaction.
follow_ups: Is TRUNCATE DDL or DML?

questions.prompt: What is paging, and how does it support virtual memory?
questions.relevance_to_role: Paging in virtual memory is listed by an editorial source.
questions.expected_answer: Memory is divided into fixed-size pages and frames. A page table maps virtual pages to physical frames. Pages not in RAM trigger a page fault and are loaded from disk. Paging avoids external fragmentation.
follow_ups: What is thrashing?
